title: Turkey & Gravy Recipe Roundup
contentHtml:
Everything you need to know about cooking the turkey this Thanksgiving Day, plus the essential gravy and cranberry sauce sides.

We've gathered everything you need to know about roasting a bird this Thanksgiving. From what to buy and how to prepare the carcass to different recipes to try on the big day, dive into our 2026 guide below.

Spatchcock is the future.

How to Buy and Prep Your Turkey

The day of Thanksgiving is a carefully managed dance through the kitchen—and that doesn't even take into account the weeks (or months!) of prep time required to make that final show possible. If you're looking for guidance on which type of bird to buy, whether it should be fresh or frozen, or advice on how handle storage and thawing, head over to the Definitive Guide to Buying Prepping, Cooking, and Carving Your Holiday Turkey. 🔗

If you're not looking for that Norman Rockwell whole-bird-carved-on-the-table look, spatchcocking (or butterflying) the turkey is a great option. By removing the backbone, you can flatten the bird for more even heat distribution, a faster cooking time, and crispier skin. You can do this before brining or day-of. Dive into the how and why behind spatchcocking your turkey. 🔗

Once you have your turkey, but before the big day, we recommend dry-brining your bird. Salting a turkey and letting it rest overnight will allow salt to penetrate the meat. This loosens the muscle fibers and prevents them from expelling as much moisture while the turkey roasts. Learn about the science behind brining in this complete guide. 🔗

My whole roast turkey setup—sans spatchcock.

Turkey Recipes to Try

Really, a good turkey doesn't need anything more than salt, pepper, some oil, and some nice browning and crisping in the oven. If you want extra flavor, the traditional advice is to make a flavored butter or oil and rub it over and under the skin of the bird. We recommend taking it up a notch by making a flavored mayo and slathering that on the bird instead. This provides a stable base for any herbs or seasonings (so they don't melt off) and contributes to the Maillard reaction (via egg proteins in the mayo). The original Mayo-Roasted Thanksgiving Turkey With Gravy recipe is available on NYT Cooking (paywalled) but you can borrow the technique from this post available on Patreon: For the Best Roast Chicken, Slather Your Spatchcock in Mayo. 🔗

Our new turkey recipe this year brings the sweet-salty-umami flavors of shio koji to the table. The deep muscle effect of salt and the surface effect of koji combine to create a tender, savory, deeply browned exterior and moist, juicy meat underneath. And because koji-brined poultry browns so easily, you can achieve complex flavors without resorting to intensely high heat and potentially overcooked meat: Koji-Brined Roast Turkey With Garlic-Scallion Mayo. 🔗

While a spatchcocked bird has its benefits, some people do want that classic Norman Rockwell look. The main trick with this recipe is to utilize a baking steel or stone in your oven to address how a turkey's white and dark meat cook unevenly. Simply swap out the roasting pan (which can further exacerbate issues with uneven cooking times) for a simple rimmed baking sheet and wire rack and pop it on the stone. This will leave you with a moist, crisp, and nicely browned bird: A Better Way to Roast a Whole Turkey. 🔗

If you're outdoorsy, smoke the bird. This low and slow approach has all the deep flavors you're looking for while avoiding dry and leathery skin. Note: This is one recipe where wet-brining is probably not the move, even if you tend to enjoy that approach; it will ultimately dilute the flavor of the turkey, so stick to a dry-brine this time. Get the guide on how to smoke a turkey. 🔗

If you're serving a smaller party, there are options for you! Using only the turkey legs, a long, slow braise in a dry red wine leaves the meat ultra moist and tender. Plus, cooking in a flavorful mixture of red wine, stock, and aromatics leaves you with a great foundation for a rich gravy: Red Wine–Braised Turkey Legs. 🔗

On the other hand, using only the breast, you can make a herb-roasted bird complete with the stuffing. A turkey breast is the ideal size for small gatherings and is far faster to cook, going from fridge to table in under 2 hours: Herb-Roasted Turkey Breast and Stuffing. 🔗

Or you can go non-traditional and make a turchetta (a turkey porchetta!). This is definitely a project that requires some time, patience, and dexterity, but that patience will be rewarded with a gorgeous, and delicious, centerpiece: Turkey Porchetta. 🔗

Rich gravy and punch cranberry sauce make the world go 'round!

Sauces on the Side

Bonus points for the spatchcock approach: You'll have a free turkey backbone you can use to fortify your gravy! For even more flavor fortification, use an umami-rich sauce or condiment (Marmite, Vegemite, Bragg’s Liquid Aminos, Worcestershire sauce, or fish sauce) during final seasoning when making this Easy Chicken or Turkey Gravy. 🔗

Following our "Warm and Koji" theme, this year's gravy recipe features Japanese curry roux cubes! Lena (head of operations here at JKLA World HQ) brought this idea back from her Canadian Thanksgiving celebration, and it was too good not to share: Turkey Gravy with Japanese Curry. 🔗

Not gravy... but a Thanksgiving table just isn't complete without cranberry sauce. If you want to gussy it up further, try adding a cinnamon stick, some orange zest, or a splash of port or Madeira if you like it a lil' vinous: The World's Easiest Thanksgiving Cranberry Sauce. 🔗

P.S. Looking for leftover turkey recipes? Stay tuned for a future dispatch!
